title: I Tested Design References on 48 AI-Generated Pages. Looking Them Up Wasn’t Enough.

What I would carry into the next test AI Agent AI Claude Code UI Design Product Management I Tested Design References on 48 AI-Generated Pages. Looking Them Up Wasn’t Enough. Ilia Popov 9 min read · Oct 26, 2026 -- Listen Share Mandatory lookup won 5 of 12 comparisons against a no-reference baseline. A workflow that also required design decisions won 8. The distinction changed what I would automate. Press enter or click to view image in full size I could require my coding agent to open design references. What I could not assume was that doing so would improve the pages. The strongest result came from the workflow that required the agent to explain what it would adapt and reject. That workflow also added deliberation, so its result does not isolate the contribution of references. With only 12 matched blocks, the result is directional evidence, not a statistically established improvement. Four workflows: no-reference control; references available, 5 wins, 6 losses, 1 undecided; required lookup, 5 wins and 7 losses; lookup plus adaptation, 8 wins and 4 losses. Each comparison contains 12 matched blocks: four briefs, each repeated three times. A block win required agreement from at least two of three model judgments. The control has no self-comparison. Press enter or click to view image in full size A tool call is an appealing success metric Inspo supplies design references through MCP. An agent can request recommendations and fetch an individual screen. Whether it called the tool is easy to count. Whether the resulting page is better requires a separate test. That question matters as designers add tools. The Tools chapter of the AI in Design Report 2026, from Designer Fund and Foundation Capital, describes average tool use rising from three tools in 2025 to seven in 2026. The report’s methodology describes a March 2026 survey of 906 designers recruited through networks and communities, with acknowledged selection bias. That provides context for the growing toolkit; it does not establish a quality benefit. I ran the fresh experiment on October 24, 2026, using four briefs: an architecture portfolio, a consultant’s quote calculator, a workshop listing, and a service-status page. Each brief ran three times under four conditions: No references: Inspo unavailable. 12 generations. References available: Inspo connected; no extra task-level instruction. 12 generations. Required lookup: Retrieve recommendations and at least one screen. 12 generations. Lookup + adaptation: Also declare three adaptations and two rejected patterns, then check the implementation. 12 generations. The first two conditions received identical task text. Tool descriptions still differed, so “available” did not mean instruction-free. Press enter or click to view image in full size The pages also had jobs to do. The calculator needed correct arithmetic and invalid-input handling; the listings needed working filters. Every page required a mobile menu and a local email-form demonstration. All 48 final-series attempts produced HTML and completed successfully. I did not repair candidates after seeing their evaluation results. The instruction that changed the comparison With references merely available, the agent requested recommendations in 10/12 runs . Both mandatory workflows retrieved recommendations and fetched a screen in 12/12. The available-only workflow made no separate screen-fetch calls. Recommendation responses can already contain images, so that does not mean those runs were visually uninformed. The adaptation workflow added this instruction before implementation: Before writing HTML, write reference-decisions.json containing exactly three concrete design choices you will adapt from the references and exactly two reference patterns you will reject, each with a reason tied to this product and its visitor. Press enter or click to view image in full size It also required a check after implementation. All 12 runs recorded the requested choices before writing HTML. That establishes declared intent, not faithful execution of every choice. Press enter or click to view image in full size Side-by-side comparison of a consultant’s quote calculator page. Left, labeled Required lookup: a centered marketing hero and three feature cards fill the first screen. Right, labeled Lookup + adaptation: the inputs sit beside a live estimate of €16,800 with one request button. Against required lookup alone, this workflow won 9 blocks, lost 2, and left 1 undecided . Against the no-reference baseline, it won 8 and lost 4. Press enter or click to view image in full size Side-by-side comparison of a workshop listing page. Left, labeled Required lookup: a search hero and undated image cards fill the first screen. Right, labeled Lookup + adaptation: a filter rail sits beside four dated rows with seats left and prices. The result was uneven across briefs. Adaptation beat the baseline in all three calculator blocks, two workshop blocks, two status-page blocks, and only one portfolio block. The portfolio result is a useful counterexample. A workflow that looked promising for the calculator did not carry the same advantage into a different design problem.
